items.title: Mercedes to run old + new car spec in Singapore amid upgrade doubts
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Mercedes is to run a back-to-back comparison between its new and old Formula 1 aero packages in Singapore to better understand whether or not its latest upgrade has worked.

The manufacturer had arrived at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia hopeful that a new development step for its W17 would lift it clear at the front of F1.

However, the expected 0.3-second improvement did not materialise, and team principal Toto Wolff reckoned it had instead dropped its performance by up to half a second.

That left the door open for Red Bull's Max Verstappen to take his first pole position and victory of the season for Red Bull.

The surprise lack of pace from Mercedes prompted some deep post-race analysis to understand what went wrong, and whether what played out was entirely down to the aero package or was linked to the rough track surface.

That work has exposed that there are areas of its car that Mercedes needs to better understand, which is why it will bring back some older specification parts in Singapore this weekend for testing.

The team will run comparison tests between the new and old parts to help build a better understanding of what has happened.

Wolff said: "We have identified several areas we need to investigate further, but F1 doesn't offer simple answers and we need more evidence before drawing firm conclusions.

"Singapore gives us an immediate opportunity to continue that work. The characteristics of the circuit are very different and that will help us build a clearer picture of where we are.

"That is why we will evaluate both the latest update package and our previous specification across the weekend to ensure we fully understand the direction we need to take."

Mercedes is due to split its old and new packages across its two cars for the entire weekend.

As the Singapore GP is a sprint weekend, there is only a single practice session before sprint qualifying on Friday evening.

The plan to do some back-to-back testing of its aero packages comes amid confirmation that George Russell will take an engine grid penalty as well, following the failure he suffered in Malaysia.

That change of components will put him at the back of the grid at a venue that is notoriously difficult to overtake on.

Wolff added: "That is particularly frustrating given the way he drove last weekend and the result he deserved to be fighting for.

"Unfortunately, these things are part of the sport and our focus now is on giving him the best possible car and opportunities to fight back through the field."

items.title: F1's cost cap fix: What's actually proposed, and for when
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Formula 1 teams are set to discuss a potential overhaul of financial regulations for 2027 aimed at ending what has been labelled a “cost cap trap” for smaller squads.

The Race has learned that the idea of a catch-up mechanism being added to the cost cap is set to be raised at the next meeting of the F1 Commission, which takes place in November.

The plan is being pushed for by Williams boss James Vowles, who wants revised cost cap rules in place for the start of next season to avoid what he thinks has become a “two-tiered” F1, where the big four teams have pulled away from the chasing pack.

Vowles sees this situation as a consequence of legacy advantages having been locked in.

Vowles fears that the more this becomes bedded in, then the bigger the risk that the divide becomes permanent.

Should teams not have the chance to mix it with those at the front, they will become less attractive for sponsors and there will be less incentive to invest. That will stop progress, lead to even worse results and see team valuations go down.

Williams is not calling for an end to the cost cap, which it thinks has been hugely positive in bringing financial stability to F1 and adding value to all the current teams because there is no longer an arms race of spending.

Instead, Vowles’ idea is to have a sliding scale catch-up system within the cost cap that allows the teams outside of the top four to spend more.

He wants it in place for 2027 because, with its impact probably going to take three years to come through the system, it needs to be there for the next rules cycle that begins in either 2030 or 2031.

The specifics of what sliding scale may be adopted depend on how talks develop within the F1 Commission or F1’s Financial Advisory Committee (FAC), but there are a few ways of doing it.

It could be implemented in a similar way to F1’s Aerodynamic Testing Restrictions, so that the team that is bottom of the standings gets the most extra allowance, with the spending freedom behind steadily reduced up until the fifth team.

Or it could be done with a tier system like happens with F1’s Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) engine catch-up mechanism. So, teams within a certain percentage range of points of the big squads are grouped together to get extra spending allowances.

Another way of doing it could be to base it on a scale that is directly related to points gaps - with it perhaps only being triggered for teams that are 100 points off the top four.

This would ensure that the system would not benefit a team that finished a close fifth and would only come into force if there was a genuine step between the 'big four' and the rest.

Is there support for his plan?

For Vowles’ plan to go through, it will need to secure support from teams in the F1 Commission.

Under F1’s current governance structure, for changes to take place at this stage for 2027, it is understood they would need support from the FIA, FOM plus six of the current 11 teams - so Williams and five others. This will secure what is known as a super majority.

However, changes to the rules for 2028 could be pushed through if there is support from the FIA, FOM plus four teams in total - so Williams and three others. This is known as a simple majority.

It is obvious that Vowles’ plan will not have universal backing – especially from the big four teams, who are unlikely to be supportive of moves that could potentially allow others to catch up.

The bigger teams are up for changes to cost cap rules, but this is more focused on pushing for areas that are currently inside the cap being moved outside.

Most recently, for example, there have been discussions about moving cybersecurity spending outside the cap.

Other squads, like Alpine, have pushed back against this and suggested that the situation should be the opposite – and all team spending should be inside the cost cap.

Mercedes thinks more thought needs to be put into how the cost cap is squeezing staff wages, as teams are limited in attracting the best staff because they cannot afford them or they are losing them to other industries.

Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: “Every team is having to trade investing in its people against investing in its car. And that's the most difficult and uncomfortable of the trade-offs that the cost cap imposes.”

The Race understands that as part of the discussions Vowles has had about his idea, four squads have indicated broad support. These teams are Audi, Aston Martin, Alpine and Cadillac.

Sources suggest Haas is against the move as the Banbury-based team is already running a tight ship and is not at the cost cap limit. Therefore, supporting any extra freedoms for spending will simply be a green light to help the opposition.

Right now, that leaves Vowles one vote short of the super majority needed to get changes in place for 2027.

Key then will be what Racing Bulls does. Getting it on board could rest on convincing Red Bull chiefs that it may be in their interest to help their second team.

Even if Racing Bulls cannot be won over, getting majority support for 2028 - so those four votes - is possible. But Vowles wants this in place for next year, so he needs to win more support.

The matter seems finely poised right now, which is why the intensity of conversations in the paddock is set to ramp up from Singapore this weekend ahead of that crunch F1 Commission gathering next month.

What is causing the 'trap'

Vowles says his experience of working at both Williams and previously Mercedes is illustrative of how smaller squads suffer disadvantages under F1’s cost cap.

That is because there is a combination of factors in play that mean smaller teams have less headroom for spending on development each year compared to the big teams – plus it costs them more to produce the same things.

As Vowles said: “One car is about 30% more expensive compared to what I remember from a previous team.”

There are many ways that this expenditure offset happens.

One example is processes and manufacturing. Big teams have been able to improve efficiency through big finance departments to make sure that there is no wastage in the system.

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen said earlier this year that key to his squad moving forward was exploiting the cost cap more as it was coming off a period of under-investment under previous owners.

He told The Race that its finance department was “under-resourced” and that “there are all sorts of areas of the budget cap which we haven't really explored properly”. “We're doing that now,” he insisted.

Nielsen said that when money was being wasted through inefficiencies in one area, that then directly limited the amount of money that could be spent on upgrades.

“If you leave stuff on the table in the budget cap, that's basically stuff that could have paid for a new front wing or a new floor or a new rear wing,” he said.

Expanding a team tomorrow to create a more efficient system for the long term is expensive. Invest a lot of money doing it, and that money has to come out of current car build and development - so results in the present dip.

Another way the bigger teams save money is by manufacturing more parts in-house. Smaller teams that do not have that luxury have to use external suppliers, which can be much more expensive.

But it is not just in cost cap spending compared to the big teams where the smaller outfits feel they are being held back.

One bone of contention has been allowances for capital expenditure, which permit teams to build the infrastructure where they can make improvements.

From F1’s cost cap coming into force in March 2020 until the end of 2025, CapEx was limited - with a broad $36 million limit from 2022-2025, although some extra concessions were given to help smaller teams in late 2023.

The system has changed since the start of 2026, but it’s still not straightforward.

CapEx limits were removed completely from the start of this year and all spending on this front was placed inside the wider $215 million overall cap.

However, any expenditure on this front has to be allocated in the cost cap through depreciation on a standardised straight-line method.

This means, for example, that if a team spends $25 million on a new windtunnel, then that money is written off over a set period. If a 10-year timescale is chosen, it would mean that $2.5 million would have to be taken into account each year.

So, if a team has made $100 million of investment on CapEx projects to improve machinery and systems, then that means $10 million more coming out of its development budget each year - compared to a bigger team that already has that infrastructure in place.

At least part of why Williams hasn’t been able to replicate McLaren’s revival is that its own infrastructures and systems had slipped badly behind the times over the last 20 years.

Whereas McLaren’s still remained very good - it was just not making the most of them.

This was proven when McLaren’s technical restructuring was initiated in 2023 under Andrea Stella’s leadership and its development work suddenly became massively more impressive even before it switched to a new windtunnel and simulator McLaren had been developing since 2019.

Williams fell much further behind the curve, which in turn held back its processes - and it was also not staffed to the same quantity or quality as McLaren either.

Even with the money from owner Dorilton, it would take time to build the team back up - and the CapEx limits were an obvious additional hurdle here, as Williams could not pump money into its factory even if it wanted to.

items.title: The 'weird' car theory sparked by F1 pecking order surprises
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Among the factors potentially behind a swing in Formula 1's recent pecking order in Malaysia is how an extreme track surface could have made some cars behave in a "weird way" aerodynamically. 

Mercedes and McLaren had claimed 14 of 15 pole positions between them prior to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and won 13 of the 15 races in 2026 so far. 

But they were comprehensively bested by Red Bull, and outqualified by Ferrari too, as Max Verstappen took advantage of F1's return to Sepang and its unique challenge to best the usual benchmarks. Even Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies admitted this was a "surprise". 

A prominent theme of the week was how the Sepang surface was unusually rough, ironically only matched by Bahrain's own Sakhir circuit, which this grand prix replaced. Mekies said the extreme heat, track roughness and layout of the track meant "most of the cars out there were out of their ideal operating window". 

An open, abrasive track surface combined with high temperatures is an established and well understood challenge, though. More interesting was a more intricate variable that hints at how that kind of surface disturbs a car's aerodynamic performance. 

Mercedes acknowledged its biggest issue was around parts of the lap where Sepang's track was its worst and most broken-up, with an emphasis on slower corners. 

Meanwhile, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was "puzzled a little bit" why its prowess in high-speed corners from recent races in Madrid or Zandvoort - the latter also utilising older asphalt - was not evident in Malaysia. 

Stella offered an intriguing hint at why this could be the case when he said: "There's some conditions, even the Tarmac conditions, they make the car operate in a weird way, not only from a tyre's point of view."

He did not want to elaborate in much detail on a technical matter but when asked by The Race if it has an aero effect and he could point to the vague areas it has an impact on, Stella replied: "I think your pointing is not inaccurate."

This is understood to relate to how loose stones in such a rough surface generate disturbed airflow so it does not behave smoothly, or as expected, along the car's aerodynamic surfaces. 

So it may be that there were moments when some cars were more sensitive to this and did not have the real-world performance or aero consistency to match the actual load teams could see in the data.

Such a phenomenon was also prominent during the previous ground-effect era from 2022-25, as those cars generated huge amounts of downforce from the underfloor but at the same time were extremely sensitive to disruptions in that airflow. 

"We think that the car operated where it should have operated to extract the downforce and the mechanical grip," Stella said of McLaren's weekend. 

"If anything, it's more about the potential of the car and we actually increased the potential of the car with the upgrades - the information we have tells us that that's the case.

"It's more the competitiveness on track that tells us, 'Oh we seem to have lost some ground' relative to the others. 

"It's difficult to understand these things.

"We need to observe the car, the upgrades and the relative competitiveness in Singapore and then we'll go with the final races."

Mercedes did not allude to something quite so specific, but deputy team principal Bradley Lord did describe it as "a bit of a 3D problem that we need to work through". 

It was - in relative terms - a disappointing weekend for Mercedes as championship leader Kimi Antonelli was only second behind Verstappen and was unable to really challenge him for the win despite jumping into the lead at the start. 

"The combination potentially of updates, track temperature and track surface caused an interaction, a set of behaviours that meant the car was not in its usual happy state, that the drivers were having to turn the car on the throttle in the slow corners," said Lord. 

"That was further exacerbating the challenges of tyre temperatures. So that's not an easy thing to unpick."

items.title: Aleix Espargaro back to MotoGP in latest Honda shuffle
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
Honda test rider Aleix Espargaro will return to MotoGP action at this weekend’s Indonesian Grand Prix, replacing fellow test rider Taka Nakagami as stand-in for the unwell Joan Mir.

Espargaro has been drafted in because Nakagami crashed out on his very first lap of the weekend last time out at Motegi and broke his collarbone.

Espargaro’s return to action doesn’t just mark his first time racing since last year’s season finale at Valencia, but it's one of the few times he'll ride a MotoGP machine since a private test crash at Sepang in April left the three-time race winner with a career-threatening shattered back.

He fell during a private outing alongside Nakagami at the Malaysian circuit earlier this year, breaking four vertebrae and needing to be medically evacuated back to Spain before requiring multiple surgeries to stabilise the fractures. 

“It is always a great honour to join the factory Honda team in MotoGP,” said Espargaro in a team statement. "I want to say thank you to them for trusting me to ride while Joan and Taka recover. 

“After the crash at the start of the year and my injury, I have not had as much time on the bike as I would like, and we travel to Mandalika with realistic expectations as I’ve had only a small number of laps and it’s a really physical track before we even speak about the weather. 

“Let’s understand how we can best help the team and Honda this weekend and focus on that.”

The former Aprilia racer spent the opening months of the year focused on Honda’s current RC213V machine, splitting duties with Nakagami while the Japanese rider concentrated on their new 2027-spec 850cc Pirelli-mounted machine until he was forced to take on double duty as test rider for both machines.

That saw him joining the factory team at the Austrian Grand Prix to replace Mir before heading to Japan as a scheduled wildcard on the current 1000cc machine, with Somkiat Chantra deputising for Mir before returning to his regular Honda World Superbike duties this weekend.

However, with Nakagami now out of action thanks to the broken collarbone he sustained at Motegi one week ago during that wildcard outing with Honda’s test team, it may well mean that Espargaro has been briefed to take it easy this weekend at Mandalika.

Another crash would leave Honda in dire straits in the final few months of development for the new bike before handing it over to their 2027 race team.

There has been no further update from Honda on Mir’s condition, with the team reporting before the Japanese Grand Prix that he continued to recuperate at home under the care of his medical team as he undergoes "a series of tests" with "the goal to uncover the root cause of a variety of symptoms the Honda HRC Castrol rider has been suffering from for several months".

items.title: The action Mercedes can take over confusing F1 upgrade
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Mercedes is keeping all options on the table, including running a potential back-to-back test with its old package in Singapore, to try to understand why its latest Formula 1 upgrade did not deliver the step forward hoped for.

However, rather than unleashing a predicted 0.3-second gain in laptime, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff wondered if it had actually resulted in a step back of up to 0.5 seconds as rival Red Bull took its first victory of the season with Max Verstappen.

Mercedes was at a loss to explain why improvements being shown on the data in terms of extra downforce were not manifesting themselves in the laptimes.

And it was particularly perplexed about why the gains it had made in high-speed corners had come at the cost of low-speed performance, and had appeared to impact its straightline speed as well.

The key answer Mercedes needs from what happened in Malaysia is how much of its performance deficit was down to the new package and how much of it was down to the unique circumstances of the Sepang event - with high temperatures and a rough track surface.

As world championship leader Kimi Antonelli said: "That's the question we need to answer because we don't really know if it made us go faster or worse.

"It's fair to say, this season that whenever we went on really old Tarmacs, we've struggled.

"For example, in Zandvoort, McLaren was much quicker than us, especially on the older Tarmac. So, I think maybe it's just a question that the Tarmac is just very old and that for the tyres it's very, very hard, and maybe we just struggle on this kind of Tarmac."

While the track surface could explain its problems in slow corners, it would not have impacted its top speed.

But deputy team principal Bradley Lord thought this was probably mostly related to extra downforce added to the car having resulted in more drag.

"That's probably one of the lesser question marks," he said. "We know that adding downforce that brings with it drag, and the calculation is that what you gain in the corners will outweigh what you lose down the straights.

"We've seen what we're expecting there, we're seeing the benefit in the high-speed corners and the medium-speed - and the drivers say they can feel it as well. 

"But there's no doubt that we've struggled in certain corners all weekend, particularly the slower ones."

Lord later said in Mercedes' post-weekend debrief: "The combination potentially of updates, track temperature and track surface caused an interaction, a set of behaviours that meant the car was not in its usual happy state, that the drivers were having to turn the car on the throttle in the slow corners. That was further exacerbating the challenges of tyre temperatures.

"So that's not an easy thing to unpick. It's a bit of a 3D problem that we need to work through, and then figure out exactly what steps we take going forward to make sure that we've got the base understanding we need to understand that the update is working well and that we're heading in the right direction in our development, not just for this year's car, but for next year as well."

Mercedes is set for some intense engineering debriefs over the next few days to try to get to the bottom of what happened in Malaysia, and work out how best to get answers for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

It is understood that the squad is open-minded about how best to tackle the issue and that nothing is off the table right now.

One possibility to fast-track an answer about what has happened could be to run the Mercedes cars in different configurations in practice in Singapore so it can gather real-world data about the gains and losses from the new upgrade.

If it concludes that the upgrade has not worked, then it is not ruling out rolling back on it long term despite the logistical complications that would cause.

Equally, Mercedes could ultimately conclude that the Malaysia showing was a one-off caused by the heat and track surface, and it sticks to pushing on with the new parts on both cars.

What Mercedes does for Singapore depends on what conclusions are found early this week. There's also the added complication of Singapore being a sprint event with only one practice session on Friday.

Lord said: "There are many things to unpick. We've seen some teams without upgrades take a step forward this weekend.

"Other upgraded teams have taken a step forward, while [some other] teams that have upgrades have performed less well than we might have expected.

"We're not the only people with some questions to answer as we leave the weekend. But certainly we've got to unpick what is down to what and understand if that has any implications on how we head into Singapore and the remaining six races after that."
