items.title: Russell at risk of 'double whammy' grid penalty
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
George Russell could face a further “double whammy” hit following his Malaysia retirement if his Mercedes Formula 1 power unit cannot be fixed.

The Mercedes driver had looked on course to take a podium finish at Sepang before he was forced to stop his car five laps from the chequered flag with a suspected engine problem.

The stoppage was a big blow to his already slim world championship hopes, as it meant the gap between himself and team-mate Kimi Antonelli has opened up to 84 points with just seven races remaining.

But worse than the setback in the standings is that the failure could further hurt his chances of beating Antonelli in the next races.

Russell is on the edge in terms of mileage with his current pool of engines, and he had been holding out for a switch to a fresh version until an expected upgraded Mercedes specification appears at the United States Grand Prix.

Mercedes is set to make use of opportunities under F1’s ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) rules to bring a new power unit homologation to Austin for all its cars.

But if Russell’s Malaysia engine is broken and cannot be fixed, then it will mean he would face the possibility of back-to-back engine penalties if he did not want to finish the season with a power deficit to Antonelli.

That is because he would need to take a fresh power unit in Singapore to get through this weekend, which will incur penalties, and then take a further hit in the following event in the United States for the ADUO step.

Mercedes still needs to properly analyse Russell’s power unit to find out the cause of his problem, but deputy team principal Bradley Lord admitted there could be some longer-term consequences.

“Yes, there may be a double whammy effect there after such a gut-wrenching blow,” he said. “It was devastating to see him have to pull off as he did.”

Lord said that there was no immediate answer as to what had triggered the issue, but he hoped it would not take long to understand.

“He came on the radio behind the safety car and said the PU started to sound funny,” he said. "We saw sensors then misbehaving and it was clear we had to pull the car over and we'd had a failure of some sort.

“We still need to understand what it means for his pool because he's not rich in low-mileage power units either. So that may mean we need to alter what had been our previous plan."

Russell described what he experienced as a “sudden failure” as he acknowledged that this had been a season where things were getting away from him.

Asked about any remaining title hopes, Russell said: “I knew that if I wanted to come back in the championship, I needed luck on my side, it wouldn't just be good performances.

“But here we are. Not only do I not have luck on my side, I've got bad luck on my side. I'll just keep fighting weekend by weekend, but of course it's exceptionally unlikely.”

items.title: Eight things we learned from F1's Malaysia weekend
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
From another Red Bull milestone to multiple teams being confused about why they were struggling, to a new flaw in the 2026 regulations being exposed, Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia taught us plenty.

Here's everything we learned from the first F1 weekend at Sepang in nine years...

F1's wet-weather problem is only getting worse

F1 has long looked allergic to racing in the rain over the last decade and the 2026 regulations seem to have made that allergy even worse.

The exact "software bug" that sent things haywire at Sepang wasn't a specific allergy to rain - the cars didn't break down directly because of the water on track. But it was the uniquely low-speed conditions created by the wet Sepang circuit that exposed the bug in the electronic control units fitted to the cars.

And it came after some already glum predictions of how the 2026 F1 cars would cope with a rain-soaked track. Isack Hadjar, who tested at a wet Suzuka earlier this year, said: "The only thing I remember from Japan is that the tyres have zero grip. It would make the racing very dangerous with a lot of water".

The delays needed for the FIA to send updated software to the teams meant we didn't see racing with lots of water - robbing everyone watching of a fascinating spectacle - and it leaves a big question: what will actually happen when these cars finally do race in the rain?

As FIA single seater director Nikolas Tombazis said: "Can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem? No, but we will do our best to avoid it."

Who knows if a first proper wet race would expose yet more problems with F1's most complicated power units ever.

Another great Red Bull F1 story achieved 

Red Bull has rattled off some astonishing F1 achievements in its journey to being one of grand prix racing’s most influential and successful entities. And it has now added another stellar chapter to its story: becoming a race-winning engine manufacturer. 

A decade or so ago, Red Bull’s engine situation was the butt of a few jokes. Not just because its partner Renault was floundering in the V6 turbo-hybrid era, but because that relationship deteriorated so badly Red Bull struck a deal to run those same engines as a customer while officially branding them as TAG Heuers. 

On the surface, we were expected to pretend there was an engine on the grid from a watch company. Well, it’s not quite the same, but now we can say (much more legitimately) there’s an engine from an energy drinks company. And it has won a race. 

Do not underestimate the scale of this challenge and success. Ford-sponsored Red Bull Powertrains has achieved something enormous by taking on, competing against, and now beating established F1 engine builders.

The investment has been immense, and the quality of the personnel sky-high, but all the right ingredients in the world guarantee nothing. Just ask Aston Martin. 

And it has also ensured Max Verstappen keeps his run going of winning a race in every single season he has competed with Red Bull. Which is not bad in itself.

Mercedes upgrade has an urgent question mark

A gain of three tenths was the internal expectation for Mercedes' major upgrade going into the Sepang weekend, but it's left it wondering whether it needs to trial it against the old package in Singapore.

Mercedes hadn't brought a major upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix in May and it probably had a car capable of winning both titles this year even without a further upgrade.

But a step forward at Sepang would have made that title run-in a lot more comfortable and provided a good platform for 2027. But that hasn't happened; instead, it's wondering if its car has actually gone backwards.

Mercedes will have some intense engineering debriefs before Singapore to understand why it underperformed in Malaysia and whether it was simply a one-off because of the Sepang circuit's particular characteristics.

The Race understands Mercedes hasn't ruled out testing its upgrade versus its old-spec car in Singapore, though that would be tricky given Singapore is a sprint weekend.

McLaren needs to understand if it’s been left behind 

Not for the first time this year, McLaren was left to rue gambling on the wrong starting tyre. But at least, unlike in Canada, it was not alone in such a misjudgement. 

The bigger concern for McLaren is that it simply lacked competitiveness at Sepang. Its point-less return in Azerbaijan was exaggerated by incidents in the race, but that was still a muted weekend and so it was again in Malaysia, where neither Oscar Piastri nor Lando Norris had the pace to do much more in their recoveries. 

McLaren was simply fourth-best behind Red Bull, Mercedes and Ferrari, and that run just a few races ago - where it was scoring poles and even wins - has ended abruptly. 

“We have to acknowledge that potentially some competitors have developed their car with bigger steps that we did,” team boss Andrea Stella admitted. 

The only silver lining is that it finished with both cars in the points at all. That could have been very different after Norris got away with a huge misjudgement behind the safety car, and only narrowly avoided taking out himself and Piastri. 

Given Norris wrongly called for Franco Colapinto to be banned for a lapse in judgement a week ago, this was a major let-off for the world champion. 

Alpine needs help to be best of the rest now

While Red Bull’s main F1 team is now a race-winning force again, sleeping on the achievements of Racing Bulls this season would be a mistake. 

Holding fifth in the constructors’ championship means the former Toro Rosso and AlphaTauri team is on course for its best-ever season across any of its identities since Red Bull bought the ailing Minardi outfit. 

In Malaysia, Racing Bulls bagged another double points finish - despite neither of its cars starting in the top 10 - while chief rival Alpine let another opportunity to score slip. 

These two teams have quite often traded having the fifth-fastest car, but Alpine has been troublingly inconsistent and inefficient of late, failing to score in three of the past six events. 

As Racing Bulls is now 22 points ahead, Alpine needs help to finish best of the rest. With the top four teams having a clear advantage, if everything goes as it should the midfielders are fighting over ninth and 10th - or three points per round. There are only seven races left and in sprints, only the top eight cars score. 

It won’t play out exactly like this, but even if Alpine beats Racing Bulls with both cars every time from now until the end of the season, it could only gain 21 points unless there’s some outside assistance.  

No team is entirely consistent through the year, as circuit characteristics vary against the strengths and weaknesses of a car and engine package, but Aston Martin and Honda have just enjoyed another wild swing.

This embattled team went from detached at the back of the grid one weekend to respectably competitive the next when a big car upgrade arrived in Hungary earlier this season. 

But a miserable - truly miserable - Azerbaijan weekend has just given way to Aston Martin’s best result of the year with Fernando Alonso finishing eighth in Malaysia. And no car or engine changes can explain that. 

Evidently the Sepang circuit, while still reasonably power sensitive, did not expose the worst of Honda’s lingering deficiencies like Baku did - in fact Honda says it even learned driveability lessons it can use running with the wet weather engine map that limits battery power to 250kW.

And the Aston Martin chassis was clearly working much better last weekend as well. The team just doesn’t fully understand why.

It also nearly fumbled its big opportunity. Aston Martin was among the teams to gamble on slicks when the race finally started, and if safety cars had not bailed it out by resetting the order, Alonso would not have had a chance to take advantage of others having messy races to steal a very unlikely eighth place. 

Now it’s on to Singapore - where Honda’s engine issues will be less of a burden once more, so if Aston Martin can really get to the bottom of how to get its car in such a sweet spot again, another opportunity surely awaits. 

Regret and confusion over Haas no-score

Haas earned its first double points finish of the season in Baku, but Sepang was a much trickier weekend - even though Esteban Ocon briefly ran as high as sixth early in the race.

That's because Ocon was on the right tyres (intermediates) while team-mate Ollie Bearman was spiralling backwards on softs.

"I ended up on slicks, and that was the wrong choice. It wasn't my choice. I was adamant that we start on inters, and there was 0% chance that we put the slick," Bearman explained after the race.

"But the team decided to put me on the slick at the last minute, which I didn't know about. Obviously, the decision was made to split the strategy. I didn't agree with it, and in hindsight, I still don't agree with it."

Bearman admitted the team "would have looked like heroes" if the strategy had paid off, but felt "a bit hard done by" to be given what he felt was the "risky strategy" when he was the lead car within the team on the starting grid.

"It was just a shame because I felt like that decision to start me on the soft totally screwed my race," Bearman added. "I lost so much race time. I couldn't do anything about it.

"I don't blame anyone. I just want to understand what we could have done better".

Team boss Ayao Komatsu said Haas decided to "split the risk" but he "regrets" not pitting Bearman as soon as the team realised how much laptime he was losing.

The subsequent safety car closed a lot of that gap back up and Ocon lost hold of his strong points position, with Komatsu explaining, "on pit entry [Ocon] went wide and our pitstop wasn’t the best [3.6 seconds], so we lost position to one of the Racing Bulls and then pushed the new tyres too hard, and from there, Esteban’s race got destroyed."

He ended up finishing behind Bearman as they came home a distant 14th and 15th, bringing Haas's recent run of strong form to a painful end.

F1 can't wait another nine years to return to Sepang

Sepang fell off the F1 calendar just before its Netflix-fuelled popularity boom, so this weekend would have been the first taste of the circuit for a lot of the fanbase - and for over 50% of the drivers.

And it did a lot right on its unexpected return. Challenging track for qualifying? Tick. Overtaking opportunities? Tick. Strategic variation? Tick. Variable weather? Tick (even if the 2026 power units couldn't handle it).

On a calendar dominated by so many new city-centre circuits, it showed the value of an old-school track. No gimmicky corners or awkward constraints to fit your circuit around, just a well-designed, old-school track that makes use of natural elevation.

There were complaints from drivers about the "character" of the aged track surface, but does every circuit need to be a polished, completely flat runway?

The one clear improvement for any Sepang return would be fan management. There were plenty of reports on social media of fans with lengthy journeys out of the circuit, even though shuttling did improve as the weekend went on.

There are no formal plans to return to Sepang beyond 2026, but it's certainly proved itself as an 'F1 supersub', ready to jump in and host whichever country's race has been cancelled.

items.title: Japanese Grand Prix 2026 MotoGP rider rankings
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
The two main MotoGP title contenders separated themselves from the field again in the Japanese Grand Prix at Motegi - but does Marc Marquez's 37-pointer warrant P1 in the rankings, or is there another candidate?

2nd 1st 1st

One of the easier P1 selections this year (and Marquez's fourth this season, for reference).

The Ducati didn't have the clear edge over the Aprilia at Motegi some may have expected - but Marquez did have a clear edge over everyone else.

Friday to Saturday to Sunday, he was simply too strong - too in tune with the various twists of the weekend with the new surface and revised allocation, too comfortable running at consistent top pace, too precise in turning P2 into P1 in both races.

1st 3rd 2nd

Championship-spec Jorge Martin is turning up here, though Marquez has shown that won't necessarily be enough.

But Friday had promised a much more damaging weekend for Martin - who needed Pedro Acosta's help to ensure a Q2 spot - and yet he turned it around completely with an "unbelievable" overnight improvement.

Excessive tyre spin cost him on Saturday - he was maybe unlucky (and maybe careless) to touch the green paint on the final lap, but was anyway lucky that other strong riders had been taken out.

Sunday, then, was really, really good - even though keeping Marquez behind for the full distance always seemed impossible.

7th 4th 4th

A throwback to both mid-2025 Enea Bastianini (the one who could briefly make the KTM work) and to Ducati-era Bastianini (who would occasionally deliver mind-bending laps at the end of the race).

The biggest breakthrough, I think, was actually in navigating Friday and then qualifying well - though probably this was just a reflection of a higher-overall level of performance by Bastianini this weekend.

When he's fast over one lap, you know he'll be fast over a race distance. And he was, with only the finest margins separating him from podium finishes.

Acosta's DNF in the sprint complicates intra-KTM comparisons somewhat, but the 14.6s gap between them at the finish on Sunday leaves little doubt Bastianini was the RC16 benchmark this time.

12th9th 12th

Fabio Quartararo has been one of MotoGP's best riders again since the embarrassment of Aragon at the end of August.

What appears to be a minor underperformance in qualifying - relative to his own standards, because he obliterated the other Yamahas again - means it wasn't a hugely eye-catching weekend, but it was a really professional one.

He rode a strong sprint in fending off Fermin Aldeguer for the final point, and was the Yamaha standard-bearer in the main race, too - though was limited by excessive fuel consumption from very early on, a common Yamaha issue but one that seems to affect him more than some of his peers.

15th 14th 13th

This was a delightful MotoGP redemption weekend for Somkiat Chantra, whose 2025 in the category quickly devolved into a waste of everyone's time - but who, though his exit was totally justified, is better than that year suggested.

He found a bike on which "everything was correct" from the first run, tweaking only some engine brake settings for a couple of corners, and was properly competitive, just three tenths off the best Honda in qualifying and beating team-mate Luca Marini.

He looked more than a little timid in the early phase of both races - and apparently got roughed up a little by Johann Zarco on Sunday, before recovering well into the points.

The only caveat is that I felt similarly good about Taka Nakagami's stand-in effort at the previous race - and I think it's fair to ask whether Honda's regulars need to do some soul-searching about the performance they're bringing to the table.

4th 6th 3rd

The roll of the dice on medium tyres for the sprint was the biggest issue with Marco Bezzecchi's weekend - as, despite not encountering the same awful blistering as fellow medium-tyre runner Jack Miller, he simply had no pace and came home in a sixth position flattered by attrition.

Good pace on the same tyre earlier in the day meant there was some logic, but the gamble backfired.

Yet equally surprising was that, having seemingly arrived into the weekend on top of Martin and the other Aprilias, Bezzecchi suddenly had no answer to his team-mate in the most important sessions.

But also, these 20 points could have been zero. He very nearly had the same crash in the damp early in FP1 that took Nakagami out of the weekend.

8th 8th 5th

Raul Fernandez came to Motegi with lingering worry about his performance at so-called 'stop-and-go' tracks this season - and was relentlessly positive about his feeling on the weekend in that context.

He was struggling on corner entry on Friday but had underlying top-10 performance comfortably and showed it on the other two days, with the grand prix ride to fifth under pressure from Acosta and Ai Ogura particularly impressive (also because he had to manage "very big consumption" on the fuel side).

9th 2nd DNF

The Sunday crash, from "just touching the throttle and losing the front" while not really pushing, took the shine off the weekend - but the Saturday podium was more valuable to Diogo Moreira and Honda than any realistic result on Sunday would have been.

"One of the most talented riders I've ever seen, riding every different type of bike," good friend Marc Marquez raved, referencing Moreira's abundance of dirt-track skill but also, of course, his performance in MotoGP so far this season.

Add to it that he was fresh off surgery to remove a screw from his left wrist, and that puts some extra gloss on the achievement.

3rd DNF 7th

At a track where so much was expected of Acosta, he places the lowest he's been in these rankings since Jerez five months ago. That reflects, more than anything, the fact that for the first time in a really long time someone within KTM had his number - which will be easier to take after the Austria win.

Acosta cannily latched on to Bezzecchi in Q2 to secure a front row start, but didn't capitalise in either race.

He says the principal issue on Sunday was simply a mismatch between his bike and the hard rear tyre - but admitted that alone can't explain "that Enea was that fast and I was that slow".

Obviously the sprint was a write-off due to the Alex Marquez induced pile-up - but he was in the firing line to begin with because he was being overtaken by Bastianini.

11th 5th 6th

Fourth of four Aprilias in most sessions, Ogura looked more like you would have expected he would at his first race back post-injury in Austria a fortnight ago - though still he was never terribly far off.

He battled locking on Friday and lacked acceleration on Sunday, which didn't help to get through on Trackhouse team-mate Fernandez (the "messy" battle with Acosta didn't, either).

But it was a healthy return of points in the end (thanks also to a strong sprint), given he seemingly just wasn't really in the groove.

6th DNF 18th

Somewhat of a 'default' ranking for Fabio Di Giannantonio, who was banged up through zero fault of his own after the multi-bike crash in the sprint.

He was putting together a fairly promising weekend before that (though left it until the last second to secure a Friday top-10), but just wasn't fit to achieve anything much after the "big hit" to his ribs and hip on the right side.

13th DNF 8th

It was a far, far, far-far-far cry from the heights of his 2025 outlier glory weekend, but did look more like the respectable Austria than the truly dreadful Pecco Bagnaia weekends that came right before.

He made a Q1 error but the pure pace was Q2-marginal at best, and the sprint wasn't going anywhere great before he so dramatically ran out of rear rubber.

In all that context, the grand prix was quite good - but the contrast to last year was upsetting for Bagnaia. "It's not a lack of feeling," he insisted. "I cannot do what the fastest riders do."

18th 10th 9th

Aldeguer, who had had leg surgery in the lead-up to Motegi in the hopes of aiding his continued recovery from the off-season femur fracture, probably should have run with Acosta and the Trackhouse riders - but made his own weekend too difficult.

He narrowly missed out on a Q2 spot on Friday - 0.004s the difference - and then botched Q1, lapping slower than the day before and placing himself on row six.

Options were limited from there, as Aldeguer made tidy but unremarkable progress.

16th 11th 10th

Marini had to salvage a "really bad" weekend, which was compromised by a seemingly innocuous early crash on Friday afternoon - that cost him a key tyre set, he lost feeling and even when the opportunity presented itself to follow Marc Marquez for a fast lap, he couldn't capitalise.

He was outmatched in Q1 again and quiet in the sprint but found joy in the hard rear on Sunday, smoothing things over with a 10th place as, somehow, Honda's top finisher - which he so often is without having lights-out pace.

21st 13th 16th

Alex Rins's weekend was unfortunately more notable for the showy lift he got from Miller than anything he could do on track.

Crashing on his first flying lap on Friday afternoon probably didn't help, but ultimately it was a Japanese GP very much in the Rins-at-Yamaha mould - outmatched badly over one lap, quietly solid in race pace, completely unnoticed.

19th 15th 14th

What fresh twists await us in the final races of the Maverick Vinales/KTM partnership, we shall see, but this was a nicely conventional return.

Vinales wasn't faster than pre-absence but nor was he, really, slower despite the lack of recent mileage - both for muscle mass and in the fact he "doesn't trust" the bike yet.

He was nowhere in qualifying but solid enough in both races, though he did run low on energy at the end thanks to Motegi's physical nature.

22nd 17th 17th

Toprak Razgatlioglu had only done Motegi in a video game before, but seemed to do OK relative to his recent form - even if qualifying is still missing completely.

He also blotted his copybook in the sprint by going off at Turn 1, but remains less bothered by any individual result (a last-lap defeat to Rins in the GP was met with indifference) than by an overall lack of feel on braking.

He says he is "still not riding relaxed", and that this is "the biggest problem".

10th 7th 20th

Just a bit of a mess overall, recovered somewhat with the three points in the sprint. Zarco was fast enough but clearly on too much of a knife edge, as evidenced by the four crashes.

Crash one was while chasing after Alex Marquez on Friday (he was very lucky it didn't cost him Q2), crash two was late on in Q2 because he "wanted too much", crash four was in the grand prix trying to set up a move on Vinales.

But crash three proved most damaging - as Zarco, by his own admission, forgot the rule about re-firing his bike at the side of the track, so was hammered by the stewards for doing so while in the opposite direction to the racing line.

That double long-lap penalty did more damage than any of the incidents.

17th 18th 11th

Brad Binder's Sunday potentially sheds some light on that of his KTM team-mate Acosta - as he and his crew also missed the mark with this hard rear tyre. He said they "toned everything down a few steps" on the set-up trying to protect the centre of the tyre, but instead just blunted his performance to little gain - as "I think we could have done three race distances on it".

So the race was under-par, and the weekend before it likewise, Binder optimistic about going through in Q1 after Friday but crashing instead (which physically limited him for the rest of the weekend) and falling again in the sprint.

20th 16th 19th

This was another weekend that Miller found really, really frustrating, the tone set by a Q1 "f**k-up" that denied him a shot at a more representative grid position.

He was one of two riders running the medium rear in the sprint - Bezzecchi's was mostly fine, but his ended up with "blisters all over".

But that was still the better race of his two. He was left very irritated by what he believed was an overly-conservative approach from his crew to setting tyre pressures - and was in serious trouble, suffering "moment after moment after moment" and then crashing (and remounting), after which he claimed the rear tyre actually cooled down and was nicer to ride.

14th 12th 15th

Franco Morbidelli was surprisingly peppy after the grand prix, which feels out of step with the end result combined with his pedigree and accomplishments as a rider - but there's only so much energy he can expend on this go-nowhere season, and I can accept that.

A deficit of 35 seconds to the winner without the same mitigation that his VR46 team-mate Di Giannantonio had in terms of injury is brutal, and the rest of the weekend was a bit better than that (particularly Q1) but not much better.

5th DNF DNF

This was one of Marquez's best weekends of the year up to Saturday afternoon, and easily his worst from there on.

I believe there's not insignificant mitigation to his role in the multi-bike crash on Saturday, as it seemed he wasn't coming in crazy hot - and was just caught out by Acosta cutting back after being overtaken by Bastianini.

But it was still an error, and Sunday - already compromised by the double long-lap - was very poor in execution, too, from the crash in the warm-up to the sudden exit from eighth in the race caused by an accidental upshift.

items.title: Podcast: Should F1 have avoided its Malaysia farce?
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
On the latest episode of The Race F1 Podcast, Edd Straw is joined by Jon Noble and Scott Mitchell-Malm to discuss the Malaysia-hosted Bahrain Grand Prix.

It was a race that'll be remembered for Max Verstappen taking his and Red Bull’s first victory of 2026, but it was also one marred by chaos at the first attempt to start it. So what caused the farcical scenes that played out?

That's the key question tackled in part one of the podcast, before Edd, Jon and Scott explain Verstappen and Red Bull's supreme - and somewhat shock - pace this weekend, ask whether Ferrari's tyre blunder cost Lewis Hamilton a shot at victory, and unpack all of the race's other big talking points.

items.title: Edd Straw's 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia F1 driver rankings
items.author: Edd Straw
items.content:
Wet weather, tyre choices, software bugs and safety cars all added up to Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia chaos at Sepang.

That makes assessing each individual drivers' performance even more critical versus the circumstances facing them, to get a better picture of who excelled - and who didn't - amid the furore.

Here's Edd Straw's final verdict on the field in Sepang:

1st · 1st

Pole position never looked in doubt, topping Q1 and Q2 then delivering two laps good enough to head Q3 with a final advantage of 0.3s.

Losing the lead at the start, primarily down to the Red Bull's trickiness off the line that meant "the engine just completely died", was the only negative of a superbly executed race in which he carved his way to the front well, made the most of the right strategy and didn't put a foot wrong.

The emphatic pace advantage over Hadjar showed that, while the RB22 was performing well, Verstappen was also extracting everything from it with his confidence in attacking the braking zones and corner entries in qualifying particularly standing out.

Pole position and victory never looked in doubt.

2nd · 3rd

Delivered the best-possible result for Ferrari in qualifying with second on the grid, and repeated that trick in the race once you factored in the early losses to taking the race-start proper on slicks.

Had a pace advantage over Leclerc throughout Saturday and Sunday.

While his recovery in the race was assisted by circumstances, he had the pace to make the most of it and would surely have been second - and a potential threat to Verstappen - with a straightforward race.

Fast and pulled off a strong recovery drive that showed his pace.

12th · 8th

With the Aston Martin-Honda package performing well, Alonso made the most of it in qualifying to put himself well up in Q2, which he described as a "miracle".

Taking the start proper on slicks meant he was in an unpromising position, but he showed consistently good pace, including on the hards, to recover to a points finish.

Drove intelligently in the post-safety-car sprint to the flag to take eighth, holding off Lando Norris's McLaren.

For once had a modestly competitive Aston Martin and showed what he can do.

11th · 7th

Top of those who exited after Q2, even with a tow from Lindblad, was a decent performance and, given the disorder in the early part of the race, Lawson deserves credit for having an iron grip on the midfield-leading slot throughout.

Although he ran as high as fourth, the cars he finished behind were all significantly quicker, meaning realistically he achieved the best-possible result.

Got the most out of tricky weekend for Racing Bulls.

3rd · 2nd

The small error at Turn 6 that led to his laptime being deleted, forcing an extra run and limiting him to one set of softs for Q3, potentially cost him a front-row shot given his compromised runplan.

While the Mercedes didn't have the pace to threaten Verstappen, any vague hope Antonelli had of closing the gap after passing Russell vanished when he had his wide moment at the final corner and ended up taking a bite of the pit entry road.

Conclusively the faster Mercedes driver, and emerged with what was probably the best-possible result in the race - although he did have a spell behind Russell after being passed after his unsuccessful defence of the lead against Verstappen.

Another weekend where he was fast and got a good result, but had a few rough edges.

6th · 6th

The comparison with his team-mate is complicated by Norris's straightline speed disadvantage team principal Andrea Stella couldn't explain but characterised as "possibly between one and two tenths of a second" after qualifying.

Didn't maximise what was possible in qualifying, ending up five-thousandths behind Norris after an untidy Turn 2 on his second run meant he had to rely on his first-run time.

Had a decent Sunday, describing it as "a hell of a lot to finish in the same place I started" and produced a strong spell on the hard Pirellis in particular on his way to a result that was probably about right for the car.

Final Q3 run was the only notable negative on a good weekend.

21st · 13th

Given he already had a five-place grid penalty, Alpine opted to take new power unit components that were always going to be required at some point, which locked Colapinto into starting on the back row.

Although Colapinto's practice running was biased more towards race preparation, he showed he had good underlying speed in Q1 by matching Pierre Gasly's time.

Colapinto's race pace was good, but he had one of those races where he was often on the wrong side of strategy decisions - starting on slicks, pitting just before the VSC was deployed for his third stop - which meant he was unable to recover to the points.

Stronger than the on-paper results suggest.

13th · 17th

Sainz was delighted with his qualifying performance on a track that didn't play to the strengths of the Williams.

Ran in the points and as high as sixth early on, but while the car wouldn't have had the pace to stay there his slide was hastened by being understeered into by Gabriel Bortoleto and spinning.

Was never going to finish in the points, but was denied being perhaps five places higher by the Bortoleto collision.

Showed good speed, crucially without repeating any of his recent errors.

22nd · 10th

Carried a back-of-the-grid penalty into the weekend, so his mission in qualifying was primarily to reach Q2 then be used to provide a tow for Lawson, which he did well.

Recovered from starting at the back thanks to taking the start proper on inters, a team call, and was in contention for a minor points position throughout, although didn't always appear to be on top of the tyre management.

Outwitted Nico Hulkenberg in their late battle to secure the final point.

Salvaged a point from unpromising circumstances.

7th · 20th

Never looked to have the pace to match Antonelli in qualifying, which was proved by the 0.240s Q3 deficit despite having two runs compared to his team-mate's one.

Capitalised on Antonelli's fight with Verstappen to pass his team-mate with a well-executed move, although he didn't have the pace to hold onto it.

The power unit problem that cost third place late on was entirely out of his hands.

Unlucky in the race but a step behind Antonelli all weekend.

20th · 19th

Perez's weekend can only be evaluated within the context of him running not only the old-specification Ferrari ADUO 1 power unit, but also it being a tired one that didn't even give its optimum performance.

Allowing for the power unit disadvantage, Perez's pace stacked up well against Bottas when you adjust for that.

The Cadillac was the slowest car by some margin, so it's no surprise Perez finished last.

Considering the ageing power unit, a good weekend.

8th · 5th

Had a consistent pace deficit to Verstappen, with the 0.428s gap in qualifying representative.

Although he had a five-place grid penalty for taking a new ICE, Hadjar ran fourth in the first stint but never showed anything like the pace of Verstappen - struggling for grip throughout, and having a formation-lap off for good measure.

While team principal Laurent Mekies obliquely referred to the fact that "not everything went well with his car", there was no clear explanation for the lack of pace - although slipping from third at the final safety-car restart to fifth behind the two Ferraris was attributed by Hadjar to the battery being lower on energy than it needed to be.

A solid result on paper, but was not at anything like Verstappen's level all weekend.

14th · 12th

Matched Alonso in Q1, but couldn't go with him in Q2 and ended up 0.346s slower.

After switching from slicks to intermediates for the start proper, made some progress but struggled with his second hard stint and lost ground.

Ultimately, didn't quite have the same all-round pace as Alonso (although there were encouraging patches) and couldn't quite force himself into the points battle.

Had a reasonable weekend in a car that at least gave him something to race for.

16th · 14th

What was characterised as a set-up error - described as an "operational" mistake by the team - that ruined FP2 put him on the back foot heading into Saturday.

Eliminated in Q1 after finally finding a good balance for the final run, which was enough to beat Ocon by a quarter of a second.

Slicks for the start put Bearman on the back foot and, given the car pace, it's no surprise he never ran higher than 13th - with the timing of the VSC allowing him to finish ahead of Ocon.

Did a decent job considering the Friday problem and race circumstances.

17th · 15th

While elimination in Q1 was no great surprise, Ocon ended up behind Bearman having been the first driver to complete his last lap on a rapidly-improving track surface.

Thrust himself into points contention with a good first racing lap and the right call to use intermediates.

Spent much of the race trying to defy competitive gravity, but a combination of pushing too hard once he switched to hards, running wide in the pit-entry road prior to a slightly slow stop, and a green-flag pit stop when others hit the VSC that was deployed shortly afterwards, added up to 15th place.

At least kept the uncompetitive Haas in the points mix for some of the race.

15th · 11th

While Hulkenberg's underlying pace meant he might have had a shot at joining Bortoleto in Q3, a mistake on his final Q1 lap meant he was eliminated.

Pitted before the start proper to bail out of starting on softs before becoming the first to choose to switch back to slicks.

Was in the mix for points, but lost out late on to Lindblad.

Fell short of the points finish that was on offer.

18th · DNF

Complained throughout the weekend about not having optimum parts available.Made an error on his last Q1 run, which cost any chance of joining Sainz in Q2.

Although he ran seventh early on, Albon's race was troubled even before he retired with a gearbox problem - thanks to a short stint after flatspotting the softs and brake struggles.

There were clearly problems, but also a few errors.

4th · 4th

Qualifying gradually slipped away from him as it progressed thanks to what he called an "aggressive" set-up choice that meant he was struggling badly with rear-tyre overheating.

Locked up and clipped the back of Hulkenberg's Audi on the first racing lap, forcing a pitstop for a new nose. While being on slicks was a mitigating factor, he was aware grip was low.

Recovered well in the race, albeit with the help of circumstances, but struggled for balance, likely as a carryover from the set-up decisions made before qualifying.

Didn't get the best out of the car and made a significant early-race error.

10th · 18th

Did a superb job in qualifying to make Q3, although the pace was probably not in the car to have beaten Gasly.

Pitted for intermediates after initially intending to take the start proper on softs, but a misjudgement in low-grip conditions while battling with Sainz that led to him understeering into the Williams meant he had to pit for a new nose and was hit with a 10-second penalty.

Floor damage from the impact meant the rest of his race was compromised.

Qualifying was superb, but early-race mistake ruined his chances.

9th · 16th

Made the most of the Alpine in qualifying, comfortably leading the midfield and putting the car in the highest possible starting position.

Threw away ninth place and lost places to an off on slicks while attempting to warm the tyres prior to the start proper, although that likely just hastened his drop back.

Never recovered from the early losses and ended up not helped by a green-flag pitstop when others were able to stop under VSC, making this race a missed opportunity.

Strong in qualifying, but off before the start proper set the negative trajectory.

5th · 9th

Qualified as well as he could have done, especially considering a straightline deficit rated by the team as 0.1-0.2s compared to Piastri.

The error under the safety car when he had to run into the gravel at Turn 1 in avoidance of the cars ahead - including Piastri - was a needless one for a driver of his experience.

Although he recovered to ninth having dropped to 11th with his mistake, after picking off Lindblad and Hulkenberg, he never managed to mount a serious attack on Alonso in the brief chase at the end of the race.

Although his pace was good, the safety-car off tanks his rating given it was an amateur mistake.

19th · DNF

Ran the Ferrari ADUO 2 power unit for the first time, which locked in a car-performance advantage over Perez for the weekend.

Felt he extracted the maximum from the car in Q1, although his pace advantage over Perez was down to speed on the straights.

Had a dismal race, accepting responsibility for the choice to start on slicks (although he was far from the only one) but spinning into the gravel on lap eight.

Early-race spin into retirement turned a solid weekend into a bad one.

How do the rankings work?

The 22 drivers are ranked in order of performance from best to worst on each grand prix weekend. This will be based on the full range of criteria, ranging from pace and racecraft to consistency and whether they made key mistakes. How close each driver got to delivering on the maximum performance potential of the car will be an essential consideration.

It’s important to note both that this reflects performance across the entire weekend, cognisant of the fact that qualifying is effectively ‘lap 0’ of the race and key to laying the foundations to the race, and that it is not a ranking of the all-round qualities of each driver. It’s simply about how they performed on a given weekend. Therefore, the ranking will fluctuate significantly from weekend to weekend.

And with each of the 11 cars fundamentally having different performance potential and ‘luck’ (i.e. factors outside of a driver’s control) contributing to the way the weekend plays out, this ranking will also differ significantly from the overall results.

items.title: Gary Anderson: F1 got lucky Malaysia chaos wasn't worse
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
When the Formula 1 cars headed off on their formation lap for the Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang, I didn't know whether to laugh or cry.

I simply couldn't believe what I was seeing and felt that a few million other people and I were just about to be robbed of what should have turned out to be a great race. Old sparring partners Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton sitting side by side on the front row was going to be epic.

The weather conditions changing at the last minute always spices things up, but cars were basically stopping everywhere.

It was all through no fault of the drivers or the teams; their hands are tied with these stupid 2026 regulations.

I'm just about fed up with complaining about them. They are so far away from what I would call racing or what a racing driver wants that it just makes a mockery of what is supposed to be the crème de la crème of motorsport.

I'm not going to go into the fact that these cars can't or aren't allowed even to venture out on the track in the wet - that's all for another day!

Today's gripe is simply about how these stupid power unit regulations and how they are implemented are basically dangerous.

How many times this year, after seeing a driver make what we thought was an error, does that driver come on the radio and say ‘I have no idea what just happened there'? We only have to go back to Baku when Valtteri Bottas went into the safety barrier on the final lap of the race. This happened because he went down the escape road at Turn 1, the car “got confused” about where it was on the track, so instead of slowing down when he pressed the brake pedal as he wanted to, it went straight on into the barriers.

If we look at the sporting regulations; Article B1.8.1 states: “The driver must drive the F1 car alone and unaided.”

Now I completely understand why the paddle-shift gear-change system complies with that requirement, as the driver has to instigate the gear change by operating the paddle. However, I am confused that if the driver is pressing the brake pedal and the car ‘decides' it doesn't want to slow down, how does that comply with Article B1.8.1?

Moving that onto what happened on the formation lap for the Bahrain GP, we have the following rules being severely tested;

Article B1.8.5 states: “At no time may an F1 car be driven unnecessarily slowly, erratically or in a manner which could be deemed potentially dangerous to other drivers or any other person.”

And Article B1.8.7 states ”Any driver whose car has a significant failure or fault which means it cannot reasonably return to the pitlane without unnecessarily impeding another competitor or otherwise hindering the competition must leave the track as soon as it is safe to do so.”

In the technical regulations, Article C1.4 states: “The stewards may prohibit the participation of a vehicle whose construction is deemed to be dangerous.

“Should the relevant information become apparent during a session, such a decision may apply with immediate effect.”

And Article C1.5 states: “F1 cars must comply with these regulations in their entirety at all times during a competition,” and Article C1.7 says “It is the duty of each competitor to satisfy the FIA and the stewards that its Formula 1 car complies with these regulations in their entirety at all times during a competition.

“With regard to power units used on a Formula 1 car, this duty and responsibility also extends to the PU manufacturer.”

If you sum those up, the driver, the teams and the power unit manufacturer's hands are tied by an inadequate understanding and, from that lack of understanding, an inadequate set of regulations.

If we just take the startline chaos we saw in pre-season testing, where the cars couldn't manage a practice start, the FIA changed the start procedure to incorporate a five-second turbo spool-up time prior to the lights coming on. This was because of the lack of understanding of how much the teams would struggle after the removal of the MGU-H.

Being the governing body, the FIA could change that and any regulation it wanted by deeming it as a safety change. Stranded cars on the grid are dangerous but it never needed to get to that point in the first place.

And back to these power units as they are now, how long do we have to wait before someone gets hurt? Just imagine the chaos that was just around the corner if the race at Sepang had actually started in dry conditions and that thunderstorm came in around lap five.

We would have had cars littered all around the track with the drivers playing with the steering wheel buttons a bit like Elton John on his piano keys; the only difference would be they would be hitting control-alt-delete.

While they were doing that, they wouldn't have been complying with either the no erratic driving rule of Article B1.8.5 or the don't unnecessarily impede others with an ailing car mentioned in Article B1.8.7.

I'm not going to go into the rights and wrongs of what happened at Sepang because, in reality, it doesn't really matter what the details of the reason it happened were. It shouldn't have happened.

However, what worries me more is that the regulation setter, the FIA, was able to come up with a software fix in a very short amount of time and install it in all cars without any depth of real-world testing. Then what other software gremlins are lurking in there, waiting to rear their ugly head?

Now's the time to act with maturity and responsibility and react to the situation we saw at Sepang. Yes the FIA say it covered that problem with a software fix, but did it fully eradicate it or is the next problem lurking just around the corner?

This was race 16 of this season. Yes, it was the first wet event, but even still, the problems we have should not be happening.

I have been saying for a long time that the driver needs to be given control of the car through their two pedals and the steering wheel. Pull or push the upshift paddle for an upshift, pull or push the downshift paddle for a downshift, turn it to the left if you want to go left, turn it to the right if you want to go right, press the brake pedal if you want to slow down; the harder you press, the more you slow; press the torque (throttle) pedal if you want to go faster; the further you press it, the more torque you get.

As far as the harvesting and deployment is concerned it is very easy to fix. You need to put the cart before the horse instead of someone inventing this 50/50% internal combustion engine to electrical torque usage. And that 50/50 split is - other than for a very short snapshot in time per lap - basically impossible when you have cars that over an average lap are requesting positive torque from say 20% through to 100% (with this the driver is basically saying ‘I want to go faster') for roughly 60% of the lap with a negative torque request (I.e. less than 10% positive torque and brake pressure) from say 20% to 100% of the maximum brake pressure seen on a lap (the driver is basically saying ‘I want to go slower') of the brake pressure for only 20% of a lap.

If you simply take those numbers you get 80% of the lap either accelerating or braking significantly, the other 20% is down to part throttle usage. If they are anywhere near correct then you either need three times the harvesting capability you have relative to deployment, or you go to a 75% internal combustion engine and a 25% electrical torque balance.

Yes, it will mean that this mythical 1000bhp and speeds in excess of 350km/h (218mph) on the straights that F1 seems to be chasing will be reduced to probably 850bhp and 320km/h (199mph), but do we really care? I remember when that 200mph in old money was seen as a great threshold to shoot at. This ratio could be optimised pre-event for each circuit by simply averaging out the balance request from the five power unit manufacturers.

After everything settled down, we still had a very good race, but we need to remember that one of the cars that stopped on that initial formation lap was Hamilton, before his Ferrari eventually restarted. After a dubious tyre choice of slicks for the restart, which basically left him over a minute behind the leader, with a little help from the VSC and then the safety car, he ended up on the podium. However, through no fault of his own or his team, his Ferrari could have ended up not even starting.

items.title: Key figure in Honda's F1 return to be replaced in 2027
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Honda will get a new racing boss next year after the retirement of current president and CEO Koji Watanabe, who helped manage the manufacturer’s official return to Formula 1.

Watanabe will be replaced as the head of Honda Racing Corporation by Keiichi Yasuda on January 1, slightly earlier than executive-level changes would typically happen in April to align with the motorsport season.

Yasuda is currently HRC’s executive vice president and representative director.

Like Watanabe, he is a company man who has been with Honda since 1990. Prior to his HRC leadership role, which included overseeing Honda’s official F1 return under the new 2026 engine regulations, Watanabe rose to be a senior figure on the communications and marketing side within Honda.

He assumed the HRC job as part of Honda’s restructuring of its motorsport efforts in 2022 when it unified its motorcycle and car racing programmes under the same entity.

That made Watanabe a senior figure and spokesperson for Honda’s enduring relationship with Red Bull to the end of 2025 and then its new engine project with Aston Martin this year.

Honda has had a dismal formal return to F1, though, suffering a lack of performance even since the chronic reliability problems that caused an embarrassing start to the season across testing and the early races.

This has at least in part been caused by Honda’s shaky commitment to F1 and its damaging decision to withdraw officially at the end of 2021 - only continuing as effectively a service partner to Red Bull, managing the engines that were frozen in homologation from 2022 to 2025.

Honda’s board then decided to re-commit to F1 for the new rules in 2026 after all, which meant attempting to revive a project that had been gutted to redistribute engineers to other programmes - thus leaving Honda on the back foot for the new regulations.

One of the consequences of this was Aston Martin claiming it only discovered late last year just how different the Honda project was to its previous, more successful era with Red Bull.

The key decision for this was made before Watanabe was put in charge of HRC, though his role inevitably made him an important figure thereafter even if his influence over the state of the project this year is hard to discern.

Honda says the change for 2027 is being made “as part of a planned periodic personnel rotation designed to strengthen the management structure in response to global transformation and to accelerate business expansion for the next generation”.

Yasuda comes from the human resources side of Honda, with an interest in its motorcycle activities, and rose to the top position in Honda's HR division prior to joining HRC in 2026.

items.title: Was it 'unfair' not to penalise stricken F1 cars in Malaysia?
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Fernando Alonso believes it was unfair that the stricken cars were allowed to start Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as "they never stopped a race" for an Aston Martin grinding to a halt this year.

There was chaos at the attempted start of F1's first race in Malaysia in nine years as several cars encountered issues, crawling or coming to a halt, for what's now been diagnosed as a "software bug" with the 2026 power units.

But it did not affect Alonso's Aston Martin Honda. He'd overtaken the ailing Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton and would have taken the restart 11th, on the fringes of the points. 

But with that start abandoned, the order was reset to that of the starting grid for the next (successful) attempt to start the race - a decision Alonso still wasn't pleased with after the race, despite finishing eighth.  

He said: "I think I had 50% DNF this year. They never stopped the race for us." 

Asked by The Race if it was unfair, Alonso said: "100%. I mean, this is motor racing…if it's a safety concern, I get it. If there are five cars in the middle of the road or whatever, we have to stop the race and we need to see what's going on. 

"But I think they were out of the race. They were out, even on the [start/finish pit]wall. They had to push it two metres, the marshals, and retire the car - like we do in 50% of the races. 

"It's the first time I see it, but right now I don't have all the info, so maybe there is a clear explanation and it's OK. I'm not too concerned."

What was going through his mind when he saw other cars stranded?

Alonso said: "The same thing that goes through their mind when they see the Aston Martin stop, I guess. Sad on one side because they have a problem, good because you have one car less in the race."

Alonso was speaking before the FIA publicly explained that there was a software bug. It sent a software update for all teams to download before the actual race start, so it's possible he'll revise his opinion in the days to come now he knows the cause of the problem.

The key difference to Alonso's DNFs - he's retired from 37.5% of grands prix this year - is that they have all been down to Aston Martin Honda's own reliability issues. The software glitch issue that struck the likes of Hamilton was an issue with an FIA-supplied software, outside of the team or drivers' control.

There are specific regulations over starting procedures being suspended, as was the case after the formation lap chaos. 

Article B5.14.1 of the FIA's sporting regulations says: "If at any time after the formation laps behind the safety car have commenced, track conditions are considered unsuitable to start the [session], the message "STARTING PROCEDURE SUSPENDED" will be sent to all competitors.

"Red flags will be shown at all marshal posts and at the control line, and the orange lights on the start gantry will be illuminated. 

"All F1 cars must enter the pitlane behind the safety car. 

"The first F1 car to arrive in the pitlane should proceed directly to the pitlane exit…All the other F1 cars should form up in a line behind the first F1 car in the order they entered the pitlane behind the safety car when the starting procedure was suspended."  

But that order is subject to change by the time the race is properly restarted, which is what allowed Hamilton to reclaim his second place.

There are rules around "Any driver who caused an aborted start and is then subsequently able to start must start from the end of the pitlane", but this didn't apply to Hamilton because the start was aborted for multiple drivers' issues, outside of their or their cars' control. 

So it could have been a different story had Hamilton spun off by himself and caused the suspended start. Instead a common-sense decsion was taken to reset things.

Aston Martin's chief trackside officer Mike Krack called it "a difficult subject" when The Race put Alonso's comments to him.

"I think it was really the only thing the FIA could have done at that point. The race had not started, so this was the formation lap. The race had not started, and they aborted.

"Obviously, we need to review the whole thing. It was a bit chaotic. I think for everyone, nobody really knew what was going on.

"But, at the end of the day, if you zoom out, I think it was the right thing to do." 

Mercedes would have also benefited as Hamilton's demise would have been a place gained for both Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, but deputy team boss Bradley Lord felt the right decision was made. 

"I think it was a slightly unprecedented situation," Lord said. 

"Likewise, formally speaking, the starting procedure hadn't happened, we were in the middle of formation laps before a call had been made, and so it felt like the, in the moment maybe if you felt advantaged or disadvantaged, it felt right or wrong, but overall it was the common sense thing to do.

"If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled-up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and was behind the safety car on a formation lap.

"I think that would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did, and it was pretty exciting when that happened."

items.title: Winners and losers from F1's 2026 Bahrain GP in Malaysia
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
A very strange start was followed by a race full of curveballs in Formula 1's 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix, held in Malaysia.

Here's our pick of the stars and flops.

Winner: Max Verstappen & Red Bull (1st)

A first pole and win of the season for Red Bull, its engine division and the absolute star of today's show, Max Verstappen.

He was almighty at every turn today. He completed a lovely, intricate move at Turns 1-3 around the outside of Kimi Antonelli early on, was absolutely rapid as the track dried, and - after a briefly alarming moment when he stopped late on and lost the lead before the Mercedes followed suit a lap later - held off Antonelli for the win.

While you wouldn't expect to see Isack Hadjar on par with Verstappen, the gap between the two Red Bulls today shows the level at which Verstappen is operating in these scenarios. The car helped, but the driver made the ultimate difference.

And a word for Red Bull Powertrains. Both Audi and Honda (for Aston Martin) have had engine struggles this year. RBPT has produced what is F1's best internal combustion engine at its very first attempt, so that's a big positive for future years as it improves its battery and deployment abilities.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (5th)

The obvious loss for Hadjar here is being mugged by both Ferraris on the four-lap shootout after the safety car at the end.

However, look earlier and the problems were already there. He was jumped by Liam Lawson at the start, and after he got that place back he rarely matched team-mate Verstappen's pace. He was as much as three seconds per lap slower at times even when he had a certain amount of clean air.

We're not expecting Verstappen-level performances from Hadjar less than two years into his F1 career, but he looked like he was driving a different brand of car today.

Remember two safety cars reset the field. He was almost 10 seconds behind Verstappen at the lap nine safety car, and 28s behind before the one on lap 42.

Loser: George Russell (classified 20th)

Such a deeply nasty ending to what was already a disappointing-but-manageable weekend.

Even before the 'grand finale' of losing third in the final laps due to a power unit issue, George Russell had suffered a couple of ignominies at Sepang - one was the qualifying defeat to Mercedes team-mate Antonelli (who was limited to one Q3 run), the other was being reeled in and overtaken by Antonelli with what looked like unbefitting ease.

If anything, the late-race issue can almost soothes a little what had come before - because there's nothing you can do. Just wasn't his weekend. Just isn't his year.

Winner: Lewis Hamilton (3rd)

Merely changing Lewis Hamilton's tyres to inters at the start may have made him a victory contender, but watching the laptimes during the race I don't think Hamilton had an answer for Verstappen or Antonelli, especially with Hamilton's ill-chosen stint on the poorer mediums, so really I believe this was the best result possible even if Hamilton reckons second was doable.

I think it would be fair to criticise another Ferrari mismanagement of a race though, because the inters were the right choice. It was only a Hamilton masterclass and a bit of luck elsewhere away from barely breaching the points.

Hamilton carved through from 16th to fifth in the second stint after a great call to stay out on his original softs and not switch to new ones under the first safety car.

Then he reduced an 11 second gap to Hadjar down to 3.5s before stopping, struggled on the mediums then nailed a pass on the faster Red Bull shortly after the final safety car when back on his favoured softs. Unbelievable performance.

Team-mate Charles Leclerc had to overcome an extra stop, for the inters early on, but when things were level he took much longer to fight through the pack than Hamilton did. He was about 15s behind before the final safety car, but getting to fourth was still a very nice recovery. One you might celebrate if Hamilton hadn't done what he did.

Loser: Williams (17th & DNF)

In a race where it ran sixth and seventh early on with the correct choice of inters at the start, everything pretty much fell apart for Williams under the first safety car caused by Valtteri Bottas's spin on lap nine.

In the double-stack pitstop which followed for Williams, Alex Albon was the second car and had to wait for his stop, costing him three positions.

Carlos Sainz, in the leading car, was tagged by Gabriel Bortoleto on the restart. A hilarious radio sequence followed where Bortoleto said Sainz left him no room and Sainz said he left all the room in the world. The 10-second penalty for Bortoleto showed the stewards' opinion on it.

That left Sainz struggling to recover from the back, and Albon was well out of reach of the points in 19th when his gearbox later broke.

Winner: Fernando Alonso (8th)

It felt like there was never any doubt, once the restart order had taken shape during the final safety car, that Fernando Alonso would score 'something' for Aston Martin. 

He is still the go-to man on the grid when it comes to a situation like that - and the only question was whether he would be able to fend off the McLaren of Lando Norris, which, of course, he was.

It's a big result for Aston Martin (not just because Alonso was over a minute off five laps in due to the starting tyre call), and a big example of the value its star driver brings when you need to simply keep the programme afloat.

Clearly, the AMR26 has improved - but things would sure have looked a lot bleaker in the results table without Alonso's endless opportunism.

Loser: Alpine (13th and 16th) 

No intra-team collision this time for Alpine but a “very painful” couple of wrong tyre calls across both cars, which left Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly well outside the top 10. 

Gasly explained: “We thought the track could dry a lot quicker. The team was willing to take the gamble, I supported it because, to me, it sort of made sense, and our worst-case scenario was still a lot better than, unfortunately, what the reality was. 

“When we went out there, we're losing a huge amount of laptime, and then it's a choice of coming back on your decision or trying to stay out there and make it work. But we tried that and unfortunately it cost us a lot of laptime. 

“Then after the virtual safety car, we had the safety car, and everything went the other way; nothing really came our way. We never could capitalise on anything, and it was just very painful.” 

Painful because Racing Bulls scooped seven points and extended its advantage over Alpine in their battle for fifth in the championship to 22 points.

Winner: Racing Bulls (7th and 10th)

OK, so things didn’t end as well as they started for Racing Bulls, considering Liam Lawson was duelling with Verstappen for the final place on the podium on the opening lap, but Lawson still walked away with the top midfield honours. 

That’s despite some frightful formation laps where Lawson didn’t have team radio.

“I knew I had no radio before I even pulled away for the formation lap, so I was very stressed because there's a lot of procedures, especially in this year's car, that you have to do, and I literally was like, no idea what's going on, no idea what mode I was meant to be in,” Lawson explained.

“I had to look at my pit board on the way by to read a certain switch change I had to do, and then it brought the radio back. So, yeah, very stressful. 

“That was probably the most alone I've ever felt, and obviously very confusing when all the cars were slowing down, but again, I couldn't talk to the team. I didn't know if I was allowed to overtake or what. Just a lot of confusion.”

Lawson bounced back from that strongly to drive to seventh place with strong pace that made him regret not defending against Oscar Piastri’s McLaren harder. 

Team-mate Arvid Lindblad picked up the final point late on by passing Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi.

Loser: Audi (11th and 18th) 

The upgraded Audi performed much better at Sepang than it did in Baku, with Bortoleto making it into Q3, but that progress didn’t translate into any points.

Bortoleto misjudged how wet Turn 2 was and went steaming into Sainz’s Williams, picking up damage on his car as well as a 10-second time penalty that ruined any chance of points.

Audi made the wrong call fitting Hulkenberg with slicks at the start, something he admitted was “too ambitious”, but that was quickly rectified with a move back to the intermediates.

It then got the timing right to go back to slicks, but the safety car coming out right after that nullified its advantage from doing so.

“I was eating my steering wheel at that,” was how Hulkenberg described his feelings. “That sucked because I was feeling brave and like a hero in that moment.

“I think we could have undercut a few people, but unfortunately, the safety car had other plans.”

Hulkenberg ultimately ended up finishing 11th - the ninth time an Audi has finished there this season.

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (2nd)

A couple of high-profile errors at Turn 15 made Verstappen's job easier today, but Antonelli's Mercedes wasn't as fast as the Red Bull and the outcome was successfully being best of the rest and extending his points lead.

That's up to 84 now, and while the race was a bit scruffy, it didn't affect the outcome. Team-mate Russell's retirement only adds to the impending feeling that Antonelli is within reach of a first title.

Even if Russell hadn't retired, Antonelli had caught and passed Russell to show he was the quicker and better driver on the day, and even if Russell hadn't retired, it wouldn't change the expectation of where the title's going, he still would have extended his lead.

Loser: Esteban Ocon (15th)

Esteban Ocon has been in strong form lately and he made the most of starting on the correct intermediate tyre for the start to jump well into the top 10 from 17th - all after he'd pulled over to the side on the original formation lap which could have ruined his race.

He made quick work of the two Williams as well, overtaking them on merit in the early running to go as high as sixth in a "mega" stint.

But that was as good as it got as the track dried and the relative pace of the Haas showed. Spirited battles, but faster cars came through and he returned back down to 15th and behind his Haas team-mate Ollie Bearman again.

Loser: McLaren (6th and 9th) 

Like Ferrari, McLaren got the tyre call wrong at the start of the race, though it at least partly rectified that on Piastri’s side by bringing him into the pits at the end of formation laps to ditch the slick tyres.

But unlike Ferrari, the McLarens didn’t have the raw pace to make the progress it would have liked, looking fourth best and vulnerable to the midfield.

Norris was caught out by the cars ahead of him braking behind Russell’s stricken Mercedes under safety car, but it looked like an avoidable error. 

It was an error that ensured he finished behind Lawson’s Racing Bulls and even Alonso’s Aston Martin Honda. 

And the meagre points tally of 10 means Red Bull is now just 18 points adrift of it in the constructors’ championship, and Verstappen now ties Norris in the drivers' points.
